title: The mental game in coach-speak
summary: Twenty phrases coaches use about the plan, the eyes, trust, pairs and misses, with their plain meaning. How to pass on the meaning rather than the image.

body.html: Coaches often describe the mental side of shooting in short images: “trust it”, “let it go”, “stare it to death”. In English these images are easy to remember. Taken word for word, they can sound odd or even wrong in another language. Below are common phrases, grouped by moment, with what a coach usually means.

The rule for translating them is simple: pass on the meaning, not the picture. Choose one short equivalent for each phrase and keep it for the whole session or tour. Then the shooter can use it as his own cue word (Cue words and self-talk).

Before the call, coaches talk about the plan: “read the target”, “have a plan”, “commit to your break point”. The plan is a conscious decision, made while the targets are shown (in Compak® Sporting, often while watching the shooters before you). Once you call, many coaches want you simply to carry out that plan and make no new decisions, as part of your pre-shot routine (the same steps before each shot).

Many phrases are about the eyes. “Soft eyes” means a relaxed, wide look (soft focus) at the pick-up point, the place where you expect to first see the target clearly. Then “hard focus” means a sharp look at one spot on the target, often its “front edge” (leading edge). “Don’t look at the barrel” means that your eyes stay on the target, while the gun stays at the edge of your vision.

“Trust it”, “let it happen” and “see it, shoot it” mean: stop checking and steering the gun, and let your trained movement do the work. Coaches also say “don’t check it” or “don’t measure it”. When your eyes go back to the barrels to check the gap, the hands often slow down with them, and the shot goes behind (stopping the gun). “Don’t ride it” is about time: it warns against riding the target, following it too long before the shot while it slows, drops or curls away.

For pairs, “two separate shots” means that each target of the double has its own plan and its own break point. “Don’t chase the first one” means: after the first shot, take your eyes to the second target instead of watching the first one break (transition).

After a miss you will hear “let it go”, “park it”, “reset” or “next target”. They all mean roughly the same: accept the miss, do your short reset and give the next target your full routine. Many coaches leave the analysis for after the round. More in Reset after a miss.

“One target at a time”, “process, not outcome” and “control the controllables” move attention away from the score, the weather and the squad, back to your own routine. More on process goals: Process goals and the score.

Many coach cues start with “don’t”: “don’t stop the gun”, “don’t look at the barrel”. Cues that say what to do instead, and what research says about them, are covered in Cue words and self-talk. If a coach uses many “don’t” cues, ask him before the session whether he wants them passed on as “do” cues, for example “keep the gun moving”. Do not change his words on your own.

notes.html: Write your fixed equivalents on a small card before the session and use them each time. If the coach invents a new image, ask him briefly what he means, then translate the meaning.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: Forget the score and the last target: give this one target your full attention.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: Before you shoot, work out its line, speed and distance, and where it is easiest to break.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Have a plan and commit to it.
phrases.meaning: Decide your points and the order while the targets are shown (in Compak® Sporting, often while watching the shooters before you), then shoot that plan without changing it mid-shot.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: Shoot where you planned; do not let the shot drift further along the line.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: Look loosely at the pick-up area; once the target appears, lock your eyes sharply on it.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: Look at the leading edge of the target, not at the whole clay or at the gun.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: Keep an intense, unbroken focus on the target until the shot.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: Your eyes stay on the target; the gun stays at the edge of your vision.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: Stop checking the lead; let your trained movement do the work.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: Do not force or steer the shot; let the swing and the shot come as you trained them.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: When the picture is right, fire without second-guessing.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: Do not follow the target too long trying to be sure; shoot when the picture is right.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: No pause at the trigger: the swing goes on through the shot.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: A pair is two targets, each with its own plan and its own break point.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: After the first shot, move your eyes to the second target instead of watching the first one break.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: Accept the miss and stop thinking about it; the next target matters now.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: Do your short routine after the shot and start the next target fresh.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: Think about doing your routine well, not about the score.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: Spend your attention on what you can change, such as your routine and effort, not on the weather, the referee or the squad.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: Shoot your own plan and pace; do not copy the shooter before you.

key_points.html: Translate the meaning, not the image
Keep one fixed equivalent for each phrase for the whole session or tour
“Trust it”, “let it happen”: stop checking and steering the gun
“Let it go”, “reset”, “next target”: accept the miss and start fresh
If the coach invents a new image, ask what he means

quiz.q: The coach says “Don’t ride it.” What does he mean?

options.text: Put more weight on your front foot
Do not follow the target too long
Do not mount the gun too early

quiz.explain: “Riding” a target means tracking it too long to be sure. The target slows, drops or curls away, and the gun often stops.

quiz.q: How should an interpreter translate “Stare it to death”?

options.text: Word for word, keeping the image
Leave it out: it is only a joke
By its meaning: look hard at the target
As a warning about the referee

quiz.explain: Pass on the meaning, not the picture: the coach wants intense, unbroken focus on the target.

quiz.q: After a miss the coach says “Let it go, next target.” What is the message?

options.text: Accept the miss; focus on the next one
Change the order of the targets
Let the next shooter go first

quiz.explain: Accept the miss, do a short reset and give the next target your full routine; many coaches leave the analysis for after the round.
